p: An application is easier to change when its dependencies point in one direction. The usual arrangement is a thin edge layer that parses input and produces output, a domain layer that holds the rules, and an infrastructure layer that talks to databases, queues and third-party services. The domain depends on nothing outside itself; the edge and the infrastructure depend on the domain. When that rule holds, the rules can be tested without a network and a database can be replaced without touching the logic.

The practical test of a boundary is the direction of the import. If a module that implements a business rule imports an HTTP framework, a database client or a logger, the boundary is already broken. The fix is to define the interface the rule needs — a function that saves an entity, a function that reads the current time — and let the infrastructure provide it. Passing those in as arguments, or assembling them once at startup, is dependency injection in the plain sense and it needs no framework.

Keep the domain free of transport types. A request object, a result set and a database row are three different shapes and collapsing them into one is what makes an application hard to change. A request arrives, is validated into a domain input, the domain runs, and the result is mapped into a response. Each mapping is a place where a field can be renamed or a type coerced explicitly, and it is also the place where a change in one boundary does not ripple into the others. The mapping functions are boring and they earn their keep over time.

Modules should be organised by feature rather than by technical kind once the project passes a certain size. A directory per technical layer with dozens of unrelated files in each forces the reader to open five directories to understand one behaviour. A directory per feature puts the route, the rules, the queries and the tests for one capability together, which matches how changes arrive. Shared code moves to a common module only when a second feature actually needs it, not in anticipation of a third.

The composition root is the single place where everything is wired. One module reads the configuration, constructs the clients, builds the use cases with their dependencies and returns the assembled application. Keeping it a leaf that nothing else imports means no module can reach around the boundary by importing a configured client directly. It is also the only place that needs to know about environment variables, which makes the configuration contract visible in one file instead of scattered across the codebase.

Finally, resist the urge to abstract early. Two similar functions are clearer than one parameterised function with a flag. A factory, a strategy and an adapter all add indirection, and indirection has a cost that is only repaid when there are genuinely several implementations or genuinely volatile behaviour. The signal to abstract is the third duplication, not the second, and the abstraction should be extracted from working code rather than designed before the code exists. Most of the architecture advice in this chapter is about keeping options open, not about picking a pattern.

Read configuration once, at startup, validate it, and freeze it into a typed object. Everything downstream receives values rather than looking up environment variables, which means the failure for a missing variable happens at boot with a clear message instead of during a request as an undefined. Validation should check presence, type and range, and should apply defaults explicitly so that the set of defaults is visible in one place. A configuration module that throws on an invalid value is doing the most valuable work in the application.

Separate configuration from secrets. Configuration is not sensitive — a log level, a port, a feature flag — and belongs in a committed file with defaults. Secrets are credentials and belong in the environment or a secret manager, never in the repository and never in a build artifact. Both arrive by the same mechanism in most deployments, but the distinction still matters for what may be logged, what may be bundled for the client, and what must be rotated. A value that reaches the client bundle is public; treating anything else as secret is a bug.

Distinguish build-time from run-time values. A value substituted by the bundler is baked into the artifact and cannot change without a rebuild, while a value read at run time can change with a restart. Which you want depends on whether the value must vary per environment for the same artifact. A single artifact promoted through environments should read its configuration at run time; an artifact built per environment may inline it. Mixing the two is how a staging URL ends up in production.

Feature flags deserve a policy. A flag is a conditional with a lifetime, so every flag needs an owner and a removal date. Flags that stay forever become untested branches that nobody dares delete. Naming flags for the behaviour rather than the release makes them easier to grep and to reason about. Defaulting to the safe state when the flag service is unreachable is what keeps an outage in the flag system from becoming an outage in the application.

Environment parity reduces surprises. Development, staging and production should differ in configuration values, not in code paths. A branch that runs only in production is a branch that is never exercised, and a database with a different version in staging is a migration that will fail when it is run for the first time. Keeping the shapes identical and the values different is the cheapest way to make staging predictive. The remaining unavoidable differences should be listed and tested deliberately.

Report the effective configuration without reporting the secrets. A startup log line with the environment name, the version, the log level, the feature flag state and the endpoints being contacted makes a bug report actionable and reveals a wrong-value misconfiguration immediately. Redact by key name, print the names of the secrets that were found rather than their values, and include the source of each value when there is more than one layer. This is one of the few logs that should always be on.

State is the source of most bugs in a user interface, and the way to reduce them is to hold less of it. Sort every piece of state into one of four kinds: server data, form input, navigation, and derived values. Server data should be cached with an explicit invalidation policy rather than copied into component state. Form input belongs to the component that owns the control. Navigation belongs to the router. Anything computable from the other three should be computed, never stored, because two copies of the same fact can disagree.

The most common anti-pattern is duplicating server state in local state and trying to keep them in sync with an effect. Fetching data into a component, copying it to another piece of state so it can be edited, and writing it back leads to three versions of the truth and a class of stale-render bugs that are hard to reproduce. Fetch into a cache, derive the display value, and send mutations back through that cache. The mutation response is what updates the cached value, and the update is atomic.

Derived state should be computed during render, not in an effect, and memoised only when the computation is measurably expensive. A filtered list, a total, a formatted label and a validity check are all derivations. Storing them and updating them in an effect is both slower and more error-prone, because the effect introduces a render where the derived value is stale. If the computation is cheap, doing it every render is correct and simpler. Measure before wrapping anything in a memo.

Where you do need a store, keep it small and shaped around the data rather than the components that read it. A store that mirrors the component tree is a sign that the state is in the wrong place. Normalising entities by id with a separate index of ids removes duplication and makes an update to one entity a single write rather than a walk through a nested structure. The selectors that read from the store are the natural place to derive, and they are easy to test in isolation.

For real-time data, decide the reconciliation policy explicitly. A pushed update can be applied blindly, merged field by field with the local version, or dropped for a refetch. Blindly applying a push races with an in-flight mutation and can resurrect a value the user just changed; merging needs a notion of which field is authoritative; refetching is simple and correct but expensive. The honest default for most applications is optimistic local application followed by a reconciliation on the next successful response, with a version or timestamp to discard the older write.

Finally, make the loading and error states first-class rather than an afterthought. A request has at least four states — idle, loading, success and error — and a fifth, refreshing, when there is stale data on screen. Rendering a spinner for all of them discards useful data and flickers; rendering nothing while loading produces a layout shift. Decide how each screen looks in each state, including the empty case, and implement the transition deliberately. The states users complain about are almost always the ones nobody designed.

A cache is a bet that the same question will be asked again before the answer changes. Every cache therefore needs an invalidation policy, and the policy is the hard part. Time-based expiry is the simplest and sacrifices freshness. Key-based invalidation is precise and requires knowing every key a write affects. Version-tagging invalidates everything at once by changing a prefix. Choosing between them is a product decision about how stale an answer may be, and it should be written down rather than inferred from the code.

Cache at the layer closest to the consumer that has enough information to invalidate. A memoised pure function is safe because its inputs determine its output. A per-request cache is safe because the request ends. A per-user cache in server memory is dangerous in a clustered deployment because the same user may hit different processes, and a shared cache is dangerous without an eviction policy because it grows forever. Naming the layer and its lifetime in the code is what turns a cache from a hazard into an optimisation.

The cache key must include everything the value depends on. Locale, currency, user role, feature flags, data version and the parameters of the query are common omissions. A missing dimension produces a correct-looking result for the wrong user, which is a security issue as well as a correctness one. Deriving the key from a single canonical function, used by both read and write paths, is the only reliable way to keep the two in agreement; a key assembled separately in two places will drift.

Cache stampedes are the failure mode to plan for. When a popular key expires, every concurrent request misses and recomputes simultaneously, and the backend sees a load spike exactly when the cache was supposed to protect it. Two standard mitigations: a short randomised jitter on the expiry so keys do not expire together, and a single-flight lock so only the first miss recomputes while the others wait or serve the stale value. The stale-while-revalidate pattern makes the trade explicit: serve slightly old data immediately and refresh in the background.

HTTP responses have their own cache vocabulary and it is worth using rather than reinventing. Cache-Control distinguishes public from private, and max-age, s-maxage and stale-while-revalidate express the policy. ETag plus If-None-Match turns a large response into a small 304. Vary names the request headers the response depends on, so a shared cache does not serve a compressed body to a client that asked for uncompressed. A correct combination of these will outperform most application-level caches because the intermediary does the work for you.

Measure the cache or remove it. Hit rate, miss rate, the cost of a miss and the memory used per entry determine whether the cache is helping. A cache with a low hit rate adds latency and memory while protecting the backend from almost nothing. Instrument the hit and miss paths, log the key on a miss when debugging, and be prepared to delete a cache that does not pay. Caches also change the profile of the system, often moving the bottleneck to the database cold path, so only a measurement tells you where you are.

Validate once, at the edge, and convert to a trusted internal type. After validation, the rest of the code can assume the shape without repeating checks, which removes defensive branching from every function. Two boundaries exist: untrusted input from users, networks and files, and output before it is rendered or sent. Validating between them rather than at every layer keeps the domain clean and the failure messages accurate. A validation that runs in the middle of a computation cannot say which field was wrong.

A schema describes both the shape and the constraints, and it should be declared rather than written as a sequence of if statements. Declarative schemas can be composed, reused across the client and the server, tested independently, and used to generate types. The properties to require are: it produces a typed result rather than a boolean, so the caller does not have to re-read the fields; it collects all failures rather than stopping at the first; it distinguishes missing from present-but-invalid; and it strips unknown fields rather than passing them through, because an unexpected field is how mass assignment attacks begin.

Coercion rules should be explicit and minimal. A query string value is always a string, so a boolean or a number must be parsed deliberately; accepting any truthy string means that the string false parses to true. Trimming should happen before length checks so that whitespace-only input is rejected, and normalisation should happen before uniqueness checks so that two spellings of the same address collide. Where a value is a number, decide whether the empty string means zero or missing, because the two choices have very different consequences in an arithmetic path.

Business rules belong in the domain, not in the schema. A schema can say that a date is a valid ISO string; only the domain can say that it must be in the future, or that an end date must follow a start date, or that a discount may not exceed the order total. Cross-field rules also produce better messages when they live where the fields' meaning is known. The schema guards the type, the domain guards the meaning, and the error message names what the person did wrong.

Error messages are part of the interface and should name the field, the reason and the remedy without leaking internals. Message codes that the client maps to localised text keep the server free of translation and let the interface choose phrasing per context. Returning a map from field path to message lets a form highlight every offending input in one round trip instead of forcing the user to fix one field at a time. A validation that returns 422 with a structured body and a stable code per field is a small amount of work that removes a large amount of friction.

Validate on the client too, but never only on the client. Client validation is a latency optimisation and an accessibility feature; it is not a security control, because the client is entirely under the user's control. Share the schema where the language allows it, accepting that some rules cannot run in a browser — uniqueness, authorisation and anything that needs the database. The duplication that remains should be the server's version being stricter, never looser.

Model errors as values where failure is expected and as exceptions where it is not. A validation failure, a not-found and a permission denial are ordinary outcomes of a well-formed request, so returning them as typed results makes the caller handle them explicitly. An exception is for a broken invariant: a missing configuration, a corrupted response, an unreachable dependency. Getting this classification right is most of what makes error handling readable, because it separates the paths the author would think about from the ones that indicate a defect.

A custom error class carries a stable code, an HTTP status and a machine-readable detail alongside the human message. Deriving all application errors from one base lets a single handler at the boundary map them to responses without a chain of instanceof checks. The code is what clients branch on; the message is what logs and humans read; the detail is what the interface needs to highlight a field. Keeping the three separate prevents a copy edit from breaking a client integration, which is a failure mode worth designing against from the start.

Timeouts, retries and circuit breakers are the three resilience primitives, and each solves a different problem. A timeout bounds how long you wait, without which a slow dependency consumes your concurrency until you are the one who is down. A retry handles a transient failure, and must be limited to idempotent operations with exponential backoff and jitter. A circuit breaker stops calling a dependency that is failing, so that recovery is possible and so that the failure does not consume your resources on every request. All three are about protecting yourself, not about making the dependency healthy.

Bulkheads limit the blast radius by separating resources. A pool of connections per dependency, a separate queue for background work, and a concurrency limit per route mean that one saturated path cannot starve the others. Without this, a single slow endpoint can occupy every available slot and take the whole service down, a failure mode often called a cascading failure or a thread pool exhaustion. The fix is not more capacity but a boundary, and a boundary that is too generous is the same as no boundary.

Degrade rather than fail. When a recommendation service is down, show the most popular items instead of an error. When a personalisation cache is unavailable, fall back to the default ordering. When a non-essential field cannot be fetched, omit it and let the screen render. Each of these requires deciding in advance which parts of the response are essential, which is a product question with an engineering answer. A system that can serve a reduced answer is available at a level the customer can use; one that requires every dependency is only as available as its weakest one.

Finally, make failures observable at the moment they happen and reproducible afterwards. Log the request identifier, the operation, the dependency, the duration and the outcome of every failure. Emit a metric per dependency and per outcome so a rising error rate is visible before it becomes an incident. Include the version of the code and of the configuration in the log so a regression can be tied to a deploy. The cost of this instrumentation is small and the alternative is reconstructing an incident from user reports, which takes far longer and is often wrong.

Injection happens when data is interpreted as code in another language. HTML, SQL, shell, regular expressions, JSON, template strings and file paths are all languages a value can escape into. The single robust defence is to keep data out of the code channel entirely: parameterise the query, pass an argument array to the process runner, escape at the point of insertion with a helper specific to the context, and use a real parser rather than string manipulation. Every attempt to sanitise by pattern-matching is a bet against the parser you are trying to outwit.

Cross-site scripting is the highest-frequency consequence and it comes in three variants: reflected, where input echoes back in the response; stored, where it persists in the database; and DOM-based, where client code writes untrusted data into an HTML or URL sink. The defence is contextual escaping at render time — different rules inside an attribute, a URL, a style and a script body — plus a content security policy that blocks inline script and unexpected origins. A CSP is a backstop, not a substitute for escaping, and the two together are what make an injection bug survivable.

Never build HTML by string concatenation. Use a templating layer that escapes by default and requires an explicit marker for the rare case where raw markup is intended, so the editor can see and review every exception. The alternative in a client application is to construct nodes with the DOM API, setting text content rather than innerHTML, which makes the escaping automatic because there is no parsing step. When raw markup is genuinely needed, sanitise it with a maintained library that understands the HTML parser's quirks rather than a homemade tag stripper.

Path traversal is the file-system version of the same problem. A filename from a user must never be joined onto a base directory without checking that the resolved result is still inside that directory. The check is on the resolved absolute path, not on the input string, because .. sequences, absolute paths, symbolic links and platform-specific separators all defeat a string test. Replacing the dangerous sequences is not sufficient; resolve, then compare the prefix, then read the file. Reject anything unusual rather than trying to repair it.

Deserialisation is a code execution surface. Parsing JSON is safe if you then validate the result; evaluating JavaScript, accepting a serialised object graph that reconstructs classes, or trusting a cookie that encodes a session is not. Never call eval, the Function constructor or a template compiler on data. Sign anything the client sends and must not alter, verify the signature before parsing the payload, and treat every field as untrusted even after a successful signature check, because a signature proves origin, not validity.

Rate limiting and size limits are part of the input boundary. A maximum body size, a maximum array length, a maximum string length and a maximum nesting depth each stop a class of resource exhaustion attack. A request that opens ten thousand nested arrays, or claims a hundred-megabyte body, or sends a regular expression that backtracks exponentially, is a denial of service delivered as valid input. Bounding the shape before parsing is far cheaper than bounding the damage after.

Authentication establishes who the caller is; authorisation decides what they may do. They are separate concerns and combining them is how a permission check gets skipped on a route that only verified the token. Authorise on the server for every operation that touches data, and base the decision on the resource and the action rather than only on the route, because the same route can act on many resources. A check that answers whether this user may edit this document must run after the document is loaded, not before, since the document's owner is part of the question.

Never store a password reversibly. A password hash should use a deliberately slow, memory-hard algorithm with a per-user random salt, and the parameters should be stored alongside the hash so they can be raised over time. Verifying should compare in constant time. The common mistakes are a fast general-purpose hash, a global salt, a home-grown scheme, and storing the parameters nowhere so they cannot be migrated. Login must also be rate limited per account and per address, and must not reveal whether the account exists through a different error or a different response time.

Session tokens must be random, sufficiently long, stored hashed on the server, and invalidated on logout and on privilege change. A token in a URL is logged, shared in a referrer header and bookmarked, so tokens belong in a header or a cookie. A cookie that carries a session must be HttpOnly so script cannot read it, Secure so it is only sent over TLS, and SameSite so it is not attached to cross-site requests. Expiry should be short with a rotation on use if the threat model warrants it, and the rotation must invalidate the previous token rather than accepting both forever.

Authorisation failures should be indistinguishable where the existence of a resource is itself sensitive. Returning not-found for an object the caller may not see avoids leaking that the object exists, which is otherwise an enumeration oracle. Where the resource's existence is public, forbidden is the clearer answer. Decide per resource and be consistent, because a mix of the two on related endpoints lets an attacker infer the difference. The rule of thumb is that a system should not confirm the existence of anything the caller has no business knowing about.

Secrets management is mostly discipline. Keep secrets out of source control, out of build artifacts, out of client bundles and out of logs. Rotate on a schedule and on suspicion, and make rotation cheap by reading the value at run time rather than baking it in. Scope each secret to the smallest set of services that need it. Prefer short-lived credentials minted by the platform to long-lived keys pasted into a configuration file, and prefer a secret manager to an environment variable for anything that must be audited. The strongest control is one that never exists on a disk.

Finally, know the classes of bug you are most likely to ship, because the list is short and consistent: broken access control on an endpoint that forgot a check, injection through a concatenated query or a rendered string, a secret in a client bundle or a log, an outbound request to a user-controlled URL, and a dependency with a known vulnerability. Each has a mechanical control — a default-deny authorisation layer, a parameterised data path, a secret scanner, an allow-list for outbound hosts, and automated dependency updates. Adopting those five controls removes the majority of practical risk and costs a few days.

TypeScript adds a static type system that is erased at run time. Nothing it checks exists in the shipped output, so a type assertion changes only what the compiler believes and has no effect on the value. That single fact explains the whole discipline: types verify the code you wrote, they do not validate the data you receive. Anything that crosses a trust boundary — a network response, a file, a form field, an environment variable — is untyped at run time no matter what annotation you put on it, and must be validated before it is given a type.

The value of annotations is that they turn an assumption into a checked statement. A function signature documents what it accepts and what it returns, and the compiler enforces it at every call site, including the ones written a year later. That is why annotating the boundaries matters most: exported functions, module interfaces, configuration shapes and API payloads. Annotating every local variable adds noise without adding information, because the compiler already infers it and the inference is usually better than what you would write.

Strictness is where the benefit lives. Enabling strict and its related checks turns null and undefined into first-class cases, forbids the implicit any that silently disables checking, and catches the function parameter variance problems that otherwise appear as a run-time error in a callback. The migration cost is real and concentrated in the initial cleanup, and the alternative is a type system that reports success while the code still throws. Start a new project strict; for an existing one, enable the checks one at a time and fix each wave rather than disabling them when they are inconvenient.

Structural typing means a value is compatible when it has the required members, regardless of where it came from. There is no nominal identity unless you create one. This makes types compose well across library boundaries and it also means a value of the wrong conceptual type can be accepted if it happens to have the same shape — a User and an Admin with identical fields are interchangeable. When conceptual distinction matters, brand the type with a phantom property that only your constructor can create, which makes the compiler distinguish two structurally identical types.

The any type disables checking for everything it touches and spreads through the program because any is assignable to everything and vice versa. Prefer unknown for an untyped value: it accepts anything in but requires a narrowing check before use, which forces the validation to be written. Where a type is genuinely impossible to express, a single carefully isolated any with a comment explaining why is better than many inferred ones scattered through the code. Treat every new any as a decision to be justified, and treat a file full of them as a file whose types are not doing anything.

Finally, keep types and values in step by deriving rather than duplicating. A union of string literals should come from the same constant array the code iterates, so adding a variant cannot be forgotten in one place. A type for a payload should be inferred from the schema that validates it, so the compile-time and run-time notions of the shape cannot disagree. Duplication between a type and a value is the mechanism by which they drift, and deriving one from the other removes the possibility entirely.

A generic parameter is a placeholder for a type that the caller supplies, and the constraint says what the placeholder must be able to do. Writing a function over T constrained to have a length property lets it accept arrays, strings and typed arrays with the correct return type. The mistake to avoid is using a generic where a specific type would do, because a generic that is only ever instantiated with one type adds indirection without adding safety. Introduce the parameter when a second type actually appears.

Keyof and indexed access express relationships between a type and its keys. A function that reads a property named by an argument can be typed so that the argument is restricted to the keys of the object and the return type is the type of that property, which removes a cast and a whole class of typo. Mapped types go further and construct a new type from the keys of another, which is how Partial, Required, Readonly and Pick are defined. Reading those definitions once is the fastest way to become fluent in the system.

Narrowing is how the compiler learns more about a value inside a branch. A typeof check, an instanceof check, an equality check against a literal and a property-presence check all narrow the type, and the compiler tracks the narrowing through sequential statements. The important rules are that narrowing does not survive a function call the compiler cannot see through, and that a mutable variable captured by a closure can be widened back on each use. When narrowing is lost, the fix is usually to assign to a const in the narrowed branch and use that.

A type predicate is a function that tells the compiler what a boolean return means. Writing a guard as a function returning a predicate type lets it be reused across the codebase and applies narrowing at every call site, which is the difference between validation and repeated inline checks. The compiler trusts the predicate, so an incorrect one is a silent lie that disables checking downstream — the classic case being a guard that returns true for a shape it does not verify. Guards should be as small and as obviously correct as possible.

Discriminated unions are the most valuable single pattern in the system. Give each variant a literal property, typically a kind or a type field, and a switch over that property narrows to each variant exhaustively. Adding a variant then produces a compile error in every switch that does not handle it, provided the default branch asserts the value is never. That exhaustiveness check converts a class of forgotten-case bugs into a build failure, and it is worth the small ceremony of the discriminator on every variant.

Utility types cover most transformations without new syntax. Awaited unwraps a promise type, ReturnType and Parameters derive a function's contract, Record builds an object type from a key union, and Omit and Pick shape an object from another. Using them keeps a derived type tied to its source, so a change propagates. The caution is that a deeply composed utility type produces error messages that are very hard to read, so when a message becomes incomprehensible, extract an intermediate named type — which improves both the message and the documentation.
